from collections import Counter

im = Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')
W, H = im.size
px = im.load()

cols = []

    r=g=b=0
    for y in range(H):
        p = px[x,y]

    n=H

# Overall stats
import statistics

n = len(allpix)

mg = sum(p[1] for p in allpix)/n

    h,s,v = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(r/255,g/255,b/255)

    if v < 0.12: return 'K'  # very dark (black-ish)
    if v > 0.75 and s < 0.25: return 'W'  # bright pale
    if s < 0.18: return 'G'  # gray

    if 230 <= hd < 290: return 'P'  # purple
    if hd >= 290 or hd < 20: return 'R'  # red/pink
    return '?'

for x in range(W):
    r=g=b=0
    for y in range(H):
        p = px[x,y]
        r+=p[0]; g+=p[1]; b+=p[2]
    n=H
    timeline.append(classify(r/n,g/n,b/n))

# Print as blocks of 50 columns = 20 rows of 50
for row in range(0, W, 50):
    print(f"{row:4d}-{row+49:4d}: " + ''.join(timeline[row:row+50]))

from collections import Counter
print(Counter(timeline))

***Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror*** ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): *Nosferatu – Eine Symphonie des Grauens*) is a 1922 [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") [German Expressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Expressionism_\(cinema\) "German Expressionism (cinema)") [vampire film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire_film "Vampire film") directed by [F. W. Murnau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Murnau "F. W. Murnau") from a screenplay by [Henrik Galeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Galeen "Henrik Galeen"). It stars [Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck") as [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok"), a [vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire") who preys on the wife ([Greta Schröder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Schröder "Greta Schröder")) of his [estate agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estate_agent "Estate agent") ([Gustav von Wangenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_von_Wangenheim "Gustav von Wangenheim")) and brings the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)") to their town.

*Nosferatu* was produced by [Prana Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prana_Film "Prana Film") \[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prana%20Film "fr:Prana Film")\] and is an unofficial and unauthorized adaptation of [Bram Stoker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bram_Stoker "Bram Stoker")'s 1897 novel *[Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula "Dracula")*. Various names and other details were changed from the novel, including [Count Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Dracula "Count Dracula") being renamed [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok"). Although those changes are often represented as a defense against [copyright infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement") accusations,[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) the original German [intertitles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitles "Intertitles") acknowledged *Dracula* as the source. Film historian David Kalat states in his commentary track that since the film was "a low-budget film made by Germans for German audiences... setting it in Germany with German-named characters makes the story more tangible and immediate for German-speaking viewers".[\[4\]](#cite_note-:0-4)

Even with several details altered, Stoker's widow, [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Stoker "Florence Stoker"), sued over the adaptation's copyright violation, and a court ruling ordered all copies of the film to be [destroyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_film "Lost film").[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) However, several prints of *Nosferatu* survived,[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1) and the film came to be regarded as an influential masterpiece of cinema and the horror genre.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Critic and historian [Kim Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Newman "Kim Newman") declared it as a film that set the template for the genre of horror film.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarriottNewman201820-8) The film entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") worldwide in 2019\.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Nosferatu* (1922)

In 1838, in the fictional [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Confederation "German Confederation") town of Wisborg,[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) [Thomas Hutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hutter "Thomas Hutter") is sent to [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania") by his employer, the eccentric estate agent Herr Knock, to visit a new client, [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok"), who is planning to buy a derelict house across from Hutter's own residence. As Hutter studies the route on a map, Knock secretly studies a mysterious correspondence in [cabalistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysticism "Mysticism") symbols. While embarking on his journey, Hutter stops at an inn in which the locals are terrified by the mere mention of Orlok's name. In his room, he finds a book about [vampires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire"), which he initially scoffs at but puts in his baggage.

After his carriage refuses to take him further than the entrance to the mountain pass, Hutter travels on foot until after sunset, when he is met on the road by a coach and rides to Orlok's castle in the [Carpathian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Mountains "Carpathian Mountains"), where he is welcomed by Orlok himself. While Hutter is eating supper, he accidentally cuts his thumb; Orlok tries to suck the blood out, but his repulsed guest pulls his hand away. Hutter wakes up the next morning to find fresh punctures on his neck, which he attributes to mosquitoes. That night, Orlok signs the documents to purchase the house and notices on the table a miniature portrait of Hutter's wife, Ellen, an image that the young man carries with him in a small circular frame. Admiring the portrait, the count remarks that she has a "lovely neck".

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Max_Schreck_as_Count_Orlok_in_Nosferatu_%E2%80%93_Eine_Symphonie_des_Grauens_%281922%29.jpg/250px-Max_Schreck_as_Count_Orlok_in_Nosferatu_%E2%80%93_Eine_Symphonie_des_Grauens_%281922%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Max_Schreck_as_Count_Orlok_in_Nosferatu_–_Eine_Symphonie_des_Grauens_\(1922\).jpg)

[Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck") as [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok") in *Nosferatu* (1922)

Reading the book that he took from the inn, Hutter begins to suspect that Orlok is indeed a vampire. With no way to bar the door to his bedroom, Hutter desperately tries to hide as midnight approaches. Suddenly, the door begins to slowly open by itself and, as Orlok enters, a terrified Hutter hides under the bedcovers and falls unconscious. Meanwhile, back in Wisborg, Ellen arises from her own bed and [sleepwalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepwalking "Sleepwalking") to the railing of her bedroom's balcony. She starts walking on top of the railing, which gets the attention of Thomas's friend Harding in the adjacent room. When the doctor arrives, Ellen envisions Orlok in his castle threatening her unconscious husband and shouts Hutter's name, which somehow Orlok is able to hear, causing him to withdraw.

On the next day, Hutter explores the castle. In a vault, he finds the coffin in which Orlok is resting dormant in the crypt and flees back to his room. Hours later, as Hutter watches, Orlok piles up coffins on a coach and climbs into the last one before the coach departs. Hutter manages to escape from the castle, injuring himself in the process, and after a period of recovery, he rushes home. Orlok's coffins are taken aboard a [schooner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schooner "Schooner"), which the sailors open only to discover rats. All of the crewmen later die, and Orlok takes control of the vessel. Not long after Hutter returns home, the ship arrives in Wisborg; Orlok leaves unobserved, carrying one of his coffins, and moves into the house that he had purchased.

Many deaths in the town follow Orlok's arrival, which the local doctors attribute to an unspecified [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)") caused by the rats from the ship. Knock, who has gone completely insane, is confined to a mental asylum, but escapes after strangling one of the wardens. Against Hutter's wishes, Ellen reads the book that he found on his journey; it claims that a vampire can be destroyed if a pure-hearted woman distracts the vampire from the approaching dawn with her beauty and by offering him her blood of her own free will; Ellen decides to sacrifice herself to stop Orlok. Knock, whom the villagers blame for the plague, is eventually recaptured and returned to the asylum. Ellen opens her window to invite Orlok in and pretends to fall ill so that she can send Hutter to fetch Professor Bulwer, a physician. After he leaves, Orlok enters and drinks her blood, but the sun rises and its rays cause Orlok to vanish in a puff of smoke. Knock, in his asylum cell, senses this and is shattered. Ellen lives just long enough to be embraced by her grief-stricken husband.

The film's final image is that of Orlok's castle, destroyed.

## Themes

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")\]

### The Other

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Other")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Nosferatu.jpg/250px-Nosferatu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu.jpg)

Hutter, discovering Orlok's true nature

*Nosferatu* has been noted for its themes regarding fear of [the Other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Other_\(philosophy\) "Other (philosophy)"), as well as for possible [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitic "Antisemitic") undertones,[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1) both of which may have been partially derived from the [Bram Stoker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bram_Stoker "Bram Stoker") novel *[Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula "Dracula")*, upon which the film was based.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Giesen_109-10) The physical appearance of Count Orlok, with his [hooked nose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquiline_nose "Aquiline nose"), long claw-like fingernails, and large bald head, has been compared to [stereotypical caricatures of Jewish people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereotypes_of_Jews "Stereotypes of Jews") from the time in which *Nosferatu* was produced.[\[11\]](#cite_note-Giesen_108-11) His features have also been compared to those of a rat or a mouse, the former of which Jews were often equated with.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Giesen_108–109-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13) Orlok's interest in acquiring property in the German town of Wisborg, a shift in locale from the Stoker novel's [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), has also been analyzed as preying on the fears and anxieties of the German public at the time.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25-14) Professor [Tony Magistrale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Magistrale "Tony Magistrale") wrote that the film's depiction of an "invasion of the [German homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weimar_Republic "Weimar Republic") by an outside force \[...\] poses disquieting parallels to the anti-Semitic atmosphere festering in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe") in 1922".[\[14\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25-14)

When the foreign Orlok arrives in Wisborg by ship, he brings with him a swarm of rats which, in a deviation from the source novel, spread the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)") throughout the town.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Joslin_15-15) This plot element further associates Orlok with rodents and the idea of the "Jew as disease-causing agent".[\[11\]](#cite_note-Giesen_108-11)[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13) It is also notable that Orlok's accomplice in conspiracy Knock is a Jewish realtor, who acts as the vampire's [fifth column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_column "Fifth column") in the [Biedermeier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biedermeier "Biedermeier") town of Wisborg.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

There were other views – writer [Kevin Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Jackson_\(writer\) "Kevin Jackson (writer)") has noted that director [F. W. Murnau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Murnau "F. W. Murnau") "was friendly with and protective of a number of Jewish men and women" throughout his life, including Jewish actor [Alexander Granach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Granach "Alexander Granach"), who plays Knock in *Nosferatu*.[\[17\]](#cite_note-Jackson_20-17) Additionally, Magistrale wrote that Murnau, being a [homosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_men "Gay men"), would have been "presumably more sensitive to the persecution of a subgroup inside the larger German society".[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13) As such, it has been said that perceived associations between Orlok and antisemitic stereotypes are unlikely to have been conscious decisions on the part of Murnau.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13)[\[17\]](#cite_note-Jackson_20-17)

### Occultism

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Occultism")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e3/Nosferatu_%281922%29_Knock-Orlok_contract.jpg/250px-Nosferatu_%281922%29_Knock-Orlok_contract.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu_\(1922\)_Knock-Orlok_contract.jpg)

A contract between Orlok and Knock

Murnau and the film's producer [Albin Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Grau "Albin Grau") gave Orlok a demonic lineage and an occult origin: Orlok is the creation of [Belial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belial "Belial"), one of the Satanic [archdemons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdemon "Archdemon"). Belial in [Psalm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_41 "Psalm 41") 41:8–10 is also associated with pestilence, with Orlok in film being a manifestation of contagion, rats pouring out of his coffins onto the streets of Wisborg, spreading [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)"). Orlok's link to Belial is also significant because Belial is "one of the demons traditionally summoned by [Goetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetic "Goetic") magicians" – making Orlok someone who practiced [dark sorcery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_magic "Black magic") before becoming a vampire.[\[18\]](#cite_note-annwnjones-18)

Orlok and his servant Knock are communicating in occult language – the documents between Orlok and Knock are written in [Enochian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enochian "Enochian"), a constructed language said to be that of the angels, which was recorded in the private journals of English occultist [John Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dee "John Dee") and his colleague English [alchemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy "Alchemy") [Edward Kelley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Kelley "Edward Kelley") in late 16th-century [Elizabethan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era "Elizabethan era") England.[\[18\]](#cite_note-annwnjones-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Movie_Magick_2018_p._52-19)

The character of Professor Bulwer in the film is named in reference to English occult novelist [Edward Bulwer-Lytton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Bulwer-Lytton "Edward Bulwer-Lytton").[\[19\]](#cite_note-Movie_Magick_2018_p._52-19) The idea of astral entities, arising from the dark thoughts of human beings, responsible for epidemics that call for blood sacrifices in order to prevent them, is also closely linked to that of the alchemist [Paracelsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsus "Paracelsus"), whose figure is partly embodied in the film in the character of Professor Bulwer (who is mentioned in the film to be [Paracelsian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsianism "Paracelsianism") himself). This is made concrete in the film in the plague epidemic that spreads through the town of Wisborg, which cannot be remedied by scientific methods, but by the blood sacrifice of a woman, thus destroying forever the dark being responsible for this catastrophic situation.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

### World War I

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: World War I")\]

Grau served in the German army during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") on the [Serbian front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_campaign "Serbian campaign"). He claimed he was inspired to shoot a vampire film by a war experience: in his [apocryphal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocrypha "Apocrypha") tale, during the winter of 1916, a [Serbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Serbia "Kingdom of Serbia") farmer told him that his father was a vampire and one of the [undead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undeath "Undeath").[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) F. W. Murnau also saw considerable action in World War I – not only as a company commander in the trenches of the [Eastern Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_\(World_War_I\) "Eastern Front (World War I)"), but also later in the air after he transferred to the [German air service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luftstreitkräfte "Luftstreitkräfte"). He survived at least eight crashes. [Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck") who portrayed Count Orlok also served in the trenches with the German army. Little is known of his war-time experience, but there are some signs he may have dealt with some form of [post-traumatic stress disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-traumatic_stress_disorder "Post-traumatic stress disorder"). Colleagues commented that he preferred to keep to himself. He was known to take long walks in the forest alone, oftentimes disappearing for hours at a time. He once stated that he lived in "a remote and incorporeal world". Thus it is considered that the turmoil of 1920s Germany and the war-time experiences of those who produced the film left their marks on the production of the film.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

As [Lotte Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotte_H._Eisner "Lotte H. Eisner"), a dedicated occultist, wrote: "Mysticism and magic, the dark forces to which Germans have always been more than willing to commit themselves, had flourished in the face of death on the battlefields" – these forces were intrinsic to the shaping of cinema's first vampires. Albin Grau himself also linked the war and vampires: "this monstrous [event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") that is unleashed across the earth like a cosmic vampire to drink the blood of millions and millions of men". Belial as well is the link between war and contagion, as Orlok is linked directly to the Black Death and many critics have linked *Nosferatu*'s disease-bearing rodents to the transmissible sickness associated with [trench warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trench_warfare "Trench warfare") in which rats flourished. As noted by [Ernest Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Jones_\(psychoanalyst\) "Ernest Jones (psychoanalyst)") in his psychoanalytic study of nightmares, vampire legends proliferate in periods of mass contagion.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Prana-Film_1.jpg/250px-Prana-Film_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prana-Film_1.jpg)

Prana Film logo

The studio behind *Nosferatu*, Prana Film, was a short-lived [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film")\-era German [film studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_studio "Film studio") founded in 1921 by Enrico Dieckmann and occultist artist [Albin Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Grau "Albin Grau"),[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1) named after a [Theosophical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") journal which was itself named for the [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu") concept of *[prana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prana "Prana")* (life force).[\[4\]](#cite_note-:0-4) Although the studio's intent was to produce [occult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult "Occult")\- and [supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural "Supernatural")\-themed films, *Nosferatu* was its only production,[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) as it declared [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy") shortly after the film's release.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a7/Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_3.jpg/250px-Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu_poster_\(Albin_Grau,_1922\)_3.jpg)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/83/Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_2.png/60px-Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_2.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu_poster_\(Albin_Grau,_1922\)_2.png)

Original promotional art by [Albin Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Grau "Albin Grau")

As a lifelong student of the occult, Grau was able to imbue Nosferatu with [hermetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermeticism "Hermeticism") and mystical undertones.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) One example in particular was the cryptic contract that Count Orlok and Knock exchanged, which was filled in [Enochian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enochian "Enochian"), hermetic and [alchemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy "Alchemy") symbols. Grau was also a strong influence on Orlok's verminous and emaciated look[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) and he also designed the film's sets, costumes, make-up and the letter with the Enochian symbols. He also was responsible for film's advertising campaign, creating movie posters and advertisements. Grau's visual style was also deeply influenced by work of the artist Hugo Steiner-Prag who had illustrated other texts with esoteric subjects, such as [Gustav Meyrink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Meyrink "Gustav Meyrink")'s *[Golem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golem_\(Meyrink_novel\) "The Golem (Meyrink novel)")* and [E. T. A. Hoffmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._T._A._Hoffmann "E. T. A. Hoffmann")'s *[Die Elixiere des Teufels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Devil's_Elixirs "The Devil's Elixirs")* (1907).[\[27\]](#cite_note-Silent_Screen_2023_p.184-27)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-J0710-0303-004%2C_Wismar%2C_Heiliggeistkirche.jpg/330px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-J0710-0303-004%2C_Wismar%2C_Heiliggeistkirche.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-J0710-0303-004,_Wismar,_Heiliggeistkirche.jpg)

Hutter's departure from Wisborg was filmed in the yard of [Heiligen-Geist-Kirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiligen-Geist-Kirche,_Wismar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Heiligen-Geist-Kirche, Wismar (page does not exist)") \[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiligen-Geist-Kirche%20\(Wismar\) "de:Heiligen-Geist-Kirche (Wismar)")\] in [Wismar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wismar "Wismar"). (1970 photograph)

Diekmann and Grau gave [Henrik Galeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Galeen "Henrik Galeen"), a disciple of [Hanns Heinz Ewers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanns_Heinz_Ewers "Hanns Heinz Ewers"), the task to write a screenplay inspired by the *Dracula* novel, although Prana Film had not obtained the [film rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_rights "Film rights"). Galeen was an experienced specialist in [dark romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_romanticism "Dark romanticism"); he had already worked on *[The Student of Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Student_of_Prague_\(1913_film\) "The Student of Prague (1913 film)")* (1913), and the screenplay for *[The Golem: How He Came into the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golem:_How_He_Came_into_the_World "The Golem: How He Came into the World")* (1920). Galeen set the story in the fictional north German harbour town of Wisborg. He changed the characters' names and added the idea of the vampire bringing the plague to Wisborg via rats on the ship. Galeen's [Expressionist style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Expressionism_\(cinema\) "German Expressionism (cinema)") screenplay was poetically rhythmic, without being so dismembered as other books influenced by [literary Expressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expressionism_in_literature "Expressionism in literature"), such as those by [Carl Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Mayer "Carl Mayer"). [Lotte Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotte_Eisner "Lotte Eisner") described Galeen's screenplay as "*voll Poesie, voll Rhythmus*" ("full of poetry, full of rhythm").[\[28\]](#cite_note-Eisner67-27-28)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/HL_Damals_%E2%80%93_Johannes_Maass_%E2%80%93_Salzspeicher.jpg/330px-HL_Damals_%E2%80%93_Johannes_Maass_%E2%80%93_Salzspeicher.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HL_Damals_–_Johannes_Maass_–_Salzspeicher.jpg)

The [Salzspeicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzspeicher "Salzspeicher") in [Lübeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lübeck "Lübeck") served as the set for Orlok's manor in Wisborg.

Actor [Conrad Veidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_Veidt "Conrad Veidt") was offered the role of Count Orlok, having previously worked with Murnau, but had to decline for scheduling reasons. In the search for an alternative the choice finally fell on the then-still-unknown actor [Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck").[\[29\]](#cite_note-29)

Filming began in July 1921, with exterior [shots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_\(filmmaking\) "Shot (filmmaking)") in [Wismar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wismar "Wismar"). A [take](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take "Take") from Marienkirche's tower over Wismar marketplace with the [Wasserkunst Wismar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasserkunst_Wismar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Wasserkunst Wismar (page does not exist)") \[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasserkunst%20Wismar "de:Wasserkunst Wismar")\] served as the [establishing shot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Establishing_shot "Establishing shot") for the Wisborg scene. Other locations were the [Wassertor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wismar_Wassertor?action=edit&redlink=1 "Wismar Wassertor (page does not exist)") \[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassertor%20\(Wismar\) "de:Wassertor (Wismar)")\], the Heiligen-Geist-Kirche yard and the harbour. In [Lübeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lübeck "Lübeck"), the abandoned [Salzspeicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzspeicher "Salzspeicher") served as Nosferatu's new Wisborg manor, the churchyard of the [Aegidienkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegidienkirche_\(Lübeck\) "Aegidienkirche (Lübeck)") served as Hutter's, and down the Depenau a procession of coffin bearers bore [coffins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffin "Coffin") of supposed plague victims. Many scenes of Lübeck appear in the hunt for Knock, who ordered Hutter in the *Yard of Füchting* to meet Count Orlok. Further exterior shots followed in [Lauenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauenburg/Elbe "Lauenburg/Elbe"), [Rostock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostock "Rostock") and on [Sylt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylt "Sylt"). The exteriors of the film set in [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania") were actually shot on location in northern [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"), including the [High Tatras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Tatras "High Tatras"), [Vrátna dolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrátna_dolina "Vrátna dolina"), [Orava Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orava_Castle "Orava Castle"), the [Váh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Váh "Váh") River, and [Starý Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starý_Castle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Starý Castle (page does not exist)") \[[sk](https://sk.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starý%20hrad%20\(hrad\) "sk:Starý hrad (hrad)")\].[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) The team filmed interior shots at the [JOFA studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannisthal_Studios "Johannisthal Studios") in Berlin's [Johannisthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannisthal_\(Berlin\) "Johannisthal (Berlin)") locality and further exteriors in the [Tegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegel "Tegel") Forest.[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1)

***Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror*** ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): *Nosferatu – Eine Symphonie des Grauens*) is a 1922 [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") [German Expressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Expressionism_\(cinema\) "German Expressionism (cinema)") [vampire film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire_film "Vampire film") directed by [F. W. Murnau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Murnau "F. W. Murnau") from a screenplay by [Henrik Galeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Galeen "Henrik Galeen"). It stars [Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck") as [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok"), a [vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire") who preys on the wife ([Greta Schröder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Schröder "Greta Schröder")) of his [estate agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estate_agent "Estate agent") ([Gustav von Wangenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_von_Wangenheim "Gustav von Wangenheim")) and brings the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)") to their town.

*Nosferatu* was produced by [Prana Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prana_Film "Prana Film") \[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prana%20Film "fr:Prana Film")\] and is an unofficial and unauthorized adaptation of [Bram Stoker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bram_Stoker "Bram Stoker")'s 1897 novel *[Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula "Dracula")*. Various names and other details were changed from the novel, including [Count Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Dracula "Count Dracula") being renamed [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok"). Although those changes are often represented as a defense against [copyright infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement") accusations,[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) the original German [intertitles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitles "Intertitles") acknowledged *Dracula* as the source. Film historian David Kalat states in his commentary track that since the film was "a low-budget film made by Germans for German audiences... setting it in Germany with German-named characters makes the story more tangible and immediate for German-speaking viewers".[\[4\]](#cite_note-:0-4)

Even with several details altered, Stoker's widow, [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Stoker "Florence Stoker"), sued over the adaptation's copyright violation, and a court ruling ordered all copies of the film to be [destroyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_film "Lost film").[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) However, several prints of *Nosferatu* survived,[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1) and the film came to be regarded as an influential masterpiece of cinema and the horror genre.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Critic and historian [Kim Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Newman "Kim Newman") declared it as a film that set the template for the genre of horror film.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarriottNewman201820-8) The film entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") worldwide in 2019\.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Nosferatu* (1922)

In 1838, in the fictional [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Confederation "German Confederation") town of Wisborg,[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) [Thomas Hutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hutter "Thomas Hutter") is sent to [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania") by his employer, the eccentric estate agent Herr Knock, to visit a new client, [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok"), who is planning to buy a derelict house across from Hutter's own residence. As Hutter studies the route on a map, Knock secretly studies a mysterious correspondence in [cabalistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysticism "Mysticism") symbols. While embarking on his journey, Hutter stops at an inn in which the locals are terrified by the mere mention of Orlok's name. In his room, he finds a book about [vampires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire"), which he initially scoffs at but puts in his baggage.

After his carriage refuses to take him further than the entrance to the mountain pass, Hutter travels on foot until after sunset, when he is met on the road by a coach and rides to Orlok's castle in the [Carpathian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Mountains "Carpathian Mountains"), where he is welcomed by Orlok himself. While Hutter is eating supper, he accidentally cuts his thumb; Orlok tries to suck the blood out, but his repulsed guest pulls his hand away. Hutter wakes up the next morning to find fresh punctures on his neck, which he attributes to mosquitoes. That night, Orlok signs the documents to purchase the house and notices on the table a miniature portrait of Hutter's wife, Ellen, an image that the young man carries with him in a small circular frame. Admiring the portrait, the count remarks that she has a "lovely neck".

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Max_Schreck_as_Count_Orlok_in_Nosferatu_%E2%80%93_Eine_Symphonie_des_Grauens_%281922%29.jpg/250px-Max_Schreck_as_Count_Orlok_in_Nosferatu_%E2%80%93_Eine_Symphonie_des_Grauens_%281922%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Max_Schreck_as_Count_Orlok_in_Nosferatu_–_Eine_Symphonie_des_Grauens_\(1922\).jpg)

[Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck") as [Count Orlok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Orlok "Count Orlok") in *Nosferatu* (1922)

Reading the book that he took from the inn, Hutter begins to suspect that Orlok is indeed a vampire. With no way to bar the door to his bedroom, Hutter desperately tries to hide as midnight approaches. Suddenly, the door begins to slowly open by itself and, as Orlok enters, a terrified Hutter hides under the bedcovers and falls unconscious. Meanwhile, back in Wisborg, Ellen arises from her own bed and [sleepwalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepwalking "Sleepwalking") to the railing of her bedroom's balcony. She starts walking on top of the railing, which gets the attention of Thomas's friend Harding in the adjacent room. When the doctor arrives, Ellen envisions Orlok in his castle threatening her unconscious husband and shouts Hutter's name, which somehow Orlok is able to hear, causing him to withdraw.

On the next day, Hutter explores the castle. In a vault, he finds the coffin in which Orlok is resting dormant in the crypt and flees back to his room. Hours later, as Hutter watches, Orlok piles up coffins on a coach and climbs into the last one before the coach departs. Hutter manages to escape from the castle, injuring himself in the process, and after a period of recovery, he rushes home. Orlok's coffins are taken aboard a [schooner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schooner "Schooner"), which the sailors open only to discover rats. All of the crewmen later die, and Orlok takes control of the vessel. Not long after Hutter returns home, the ship arrives in Wisborg; Orlok leaves unobserved, carrying one of his coffins, and moves into the house that he had purchased.

Many deaths in the town follow Orlok's arrival, which the local doctors attribute to an unspecified [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)") caused by the rats from the ship. Knock, who has gone completely insane, is confined to a mental asylum, but escapes after strangling one of the wardens. Against Hutter's wishes, Ellen reads the book that he found on his journey; it claims that a vampire can be destroyed if a pure-hearted woman distracts the vampire from the approaching dawn with her beauty and by offering him her blood of her own free will; Ellen decides to sacrifice herself to stop Orlok. Knock, whom the villagers blame for the plague, is eventually recaptured and returned to the asylum. Ellen opens her window to invite Orlok in and pretends to fall ill so that she can send Hutter to fetch Professor Bulwer, a physician. After he leaves, Orlok enters and drinks her blood, but the sun rises and its rays cause Orlok to vanish in a puff of smoke. Knock, in his asylum cell, senses this and is shattered. Ellen lives just long enough to be embraced by her grief-stricken husband.

The film's final image is that of Orlok's castle, destroyed.

## Themes

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")\]

### The Other

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Other")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Nosferatu.jpg/250px-Nosferatu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu.jpg)

Hutter, discovering Orlok's true nature

*Nosferatu* has been noted for its themes regarding fear of [the Other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Other_\(philosophy\) "Other (philosophy)"), as well as for possible [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitic "Antisemitic") undertones,[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1) both of which may have been partially derived from the [Bram Stoker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bram_Stoker "Bram Stoker") novel *[Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula "Dracula")*, upon which the film was based.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Giesen_109-10) The physical appearance of Count Orlok, with his [hooked nose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquiline_nose "Aquiline nose"), long claw-like fingernails, and large bald head, has been compared to [stereotypical caricatures of Jewish people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereotypes_of_Jews "Stereotypes of Jews") from the time in which *Nosferatu* was produced.[\[11\]](#cite_note-Giesen_108-11) His features have also been compared to those of a rat or a mouse, the former of which Jews were often equated with.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Giesen_108–109-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13) Orlok's interest in acquiring property in the German town of Wisborg, a shift in locale from the Stoker novel's [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), has also been analyzed as preying on the fears and anxieties of the German public at the time.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25-14) Professor [Tony Magistrale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Magistrale "Tony Magistrale") wrote that the film's depiction of an "invasion of the [German homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weimar_Republic "Weimar Republic") by an outside force \[...\] poses disquieting parallels to the anti-Semitic atmosphere festering in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe") in 1922".[\[14\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25-14)

When the foreign Orlok arrives in Wisborg by ship, he brings with him a swarm of rats which, in a deviation from the source novel, spread the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)") throughout the town.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Joslin_15-15) This plot element further associates Orlok with rodents and the idea of the "Jew as disease-causing agent".[\[11\]](#cite_note-Giesen_108-11)[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13) It is also notable that Orlok's accomplice in conspiracy Knock is a Jewish realtor, who acts as the vampire's [fifth column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_column "Fifth column") in the [Biedermeier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biedermeier "Biedermeier") town of Wisborg.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

There were other views – writer [Kevin Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Jackson_\(writer\) "Kevin Jackson (writer)") has noted that director [F. W. Murnau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._W._Murnau "F. W. Murnau") "was friendly with and protective of a number of Jewish men and women" throughout his life, including Jewish actor [Alexander Granach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Granach "Alexander Granach"), who plays Knock in *Nosferatu*.[\[17\]](#cite_note-Jackson_20-17) Additionally, Magistrale wrote that Murnau, being a [homosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_men "Gay men"), would have been "presumably more sensitive to the persecution of a subgroup inside the larger German society".[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13) As such, it has been said that perceived associations between Orlok and antisemitic stereotypes are unlikely to have been conscious decisions on the part of Murnau.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Magistrale_25–26-13)[\[17\]](#cite_note-Jackson_20-17)

### Occultism

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Occultism")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e3/Nosferatu_%281922%29_Knock-Orlok_contract.jpg/250px-Nosferatu_%281922%29_Knock-Orlok_contract.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu_\(1922\)_Knock-Orlok_contract.jpg)

A contract between Orlok and Knock

Murnau and the film's producer [Albin Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Grau "Albin Grau") gave Orlok a demonic lineage and an occult origin: Orlok is the creation of [Belial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belial "Belial"), one of the Satanic [archdemons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdemon "Archdemon"). Belial in [Psalm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_41 "Psalm 41") 41:8–10 is also associated with pestilence, with Orlok in film being a manifestation of contagion, rats pouring out of his coffins onto the streets of Wisborg, spreading [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_\(disease\) "Plague (disease)"). Orlok's link to Belial is also significant because Belial is "one of the demons traditionally summoned by [Goetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetic "Goetic") magicians" – making Orlok someone who practiced [dark sorcery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_magic "Black magic") before becoming a vampire.[\[18\]](#cite_note-annwnjones-18)

Orlok and his servant Knock are communicating in occult language – the documents between Orlok and Knock are written in [Enochian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enochian "Enochian"), a constructed language said to be that of the angels, which was recorded in the private journals of English occultist [John Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dee "John Dee") and his colleague English [alchemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy "Alchemy") [Edward Kelley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Kelley "Edward Kelley") in late 16th-century [Elizabethan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era "Elizabethan era") England.[\[18\]](#cite_note-annwnjones-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Movie_Magick_2018_p._52-19)

The character of Professor Bulwer in the film is named in reference to English occult novelist [Edward Bulwer-Lytton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Bulwer-Lytton "Edward Bulwer-Lytton").[\[19\]](#cite_note-Movie_Magick_2018_p._52-19) The idea of astral entities, arising from the dark thoughts of human beings, responsible for epidemics that call for blood sacrifices in order to prevent them, is also closely linked to that of the alchemist [Paracelsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsus "Paracelsus"), whose figure is partly embodied in the film in the character of Professor Bulwer (who is mentioned in the film to be [Paracelsian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsianism "Paracelsianism") himself). This is made concrete in the film in the plague epidemic that spreads through the town of Wisborg, which cannot be remedied by scientific methods, but by the blood sacrifice of a woman, thus destroying forever the dark being responsible for this catastrophic situation.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

### World War I

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: World War I")\]

Grau served in the German army during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") on the [Serbian front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_campaign "Serbian campaign"). He claimed he was inspired to shoot a vampire film by a war experience: in his [apocryphal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocrypha "Apocrypha") tale, during the winter of 1916, a [Serbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Serbia "Kingdom of Serbia") farmer told him that his father was a vampire and one of the [undead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undeath "Undeath").[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) F. W. Murnau also saw considerable action in World War I – not only as a company commander in the trenches of the [Eastern Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_\(World_War_I\) "Eastern Front (World War I)"), but also later in the air after he transferred to the [German air service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luftstreitkräfte "Luftstreitkräfte"). He survived at least eight crashes. [Max Schreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Schreck "Max Schreck") who portrayed Count Orlok also served in the trenches with the German army. Little is known of his war-time experience, but there are some signs he may have dealt with some form of [post-traumatic stress disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-traumatic_stress_disorder "Post-traumatic stress disorder"). Colleagues commented that he preferred to keep to himself. He was known to take long walks in the forest alone, oftentimes disappearing for hours at a time. He once stated that he lived in "a remote and incorporeal world". Thus it is considered that the turmoil of 1920s Germany and the war-time experiences of those who produced the film left their marks on the production of the film.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

As [Lotte Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotte_H._Eisner "Lotte H. Eisner"), a dedicated occultist, wrote: "Mysticism and magic, the dark forces to which Germans have always been more than willing to commit themselves, had flourished in the face of death on the battlefields" – these forces were intrinsic to the shaping of cinema's first vampires. Albin Grau himself also linked the war and vampires: "this monstrous [event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") that is unleashed across the earth like a cosmic vampire to drink the blood of millions and millions of men". Belial as well is the link between war and contagion, as Orlok is linked directly to the Black Death and many critics have linked *Nosferatu*'s disease-bearing rodents to the transmissible sickness associated with [trench warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trench_warfare "Trench warfare") in which rats flourished. As noted by [Ernest Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Jones_\(psychoanalyst\) "Ernest Jones (psychoanalyst)") in his psychoanalytic study of nightmares, vampire legends proliferate in periods of mass contagion.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nosferatu&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Prana-Film_1.jpg/250px-Prana-Film_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prana-Film_1.jpg)

Prana Film logo

The studio behind *Nosferatu*, Prana Film, was a short-lived [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film")\-era German [film studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_studio "Film studio") founded in 1921 by Enrico Dieckmann and occultist artist [Albin Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Grau "Albin Grau"),[\[1\]](#cite_note-BrentonFilm-1) named after a [Theosophical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") journal which was itself named for the [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu") concept of *[prana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prana "Prana")* (life force).[\[4\]](#cite_note-:0-4) Although the studio's intent was to produce [occult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult "Occult")\- and [supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural "Supernatural")\-themed films, *Nosferatu* was its only production,[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) as it declared [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy") shortly after the film's release.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a7/Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_3.jpg/250px-Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu_poster_\(Albin_Grau,_1922\)_3.jpg)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/83/Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_2.png/60px-Nosferatu_poster_%28Albin_Grau%2C_1922%29_2.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nosferatu_poster_\(Albin_Grau,_1922\)_2.png)

Original promotional art by [Albin Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Grau "Albin Grau")

As a lifelong student of the occult, Grau was able to imbue Nosferatu with [hermetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermeticism "Hermeticism") and mystical undertones.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) One example in particular was the cryptic contract that Count Orlok and Knock exchanged, which was filled in [Enochian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enochian "Enochian"), hermetic and [alchemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy "Alchemy") symbols. Grau was also a strong influence on Orlok's verminous and emaciated look[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) and he also designed the film's sets, costumes, make-up and the letter with the Enochian symbols. He also was responsible for film's advertising campaign, creating movie posters and advertisements. Grau's visual style was also deeply influenced by work of the artist Hugo Steiner-Prag who had illustrated other texts with esoteric subjects, such as [Gustav Meyrink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Meyrink "Gustav Meyrink")'s *[Golem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golem_\(Meyrink_novel\) "The Golem (Meyrink novel)")* and [E. T. A. Hoffmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._T._A._Hoffmann "E. T. A. Hoffmann")'s *[Die Elixiere des Teufels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Devil's_Elixirs "The Devil's Elixirs")* (1907).[\[27\]](#cite_note-Silent_Screen_2023_p.184-27)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-J0710-0303-004%2C_Wismar%2C_Heiliggeistkirche.jpg/330px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-J0710-0303-004%2C_Wismar%2C_Heiliggeistkirche.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-J0710-0303-004,_Wismar,_Heiliggeistkirche.jpg)

Hutter's departure from Wisborg was filmed in the yard of [Heiligen-Geist-Kirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiligen-Geist-Kirche,_Wismar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Heiligen-Geist-Kirche, Wismar (page does not exist)") \[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiligen-Geist-Kirche%20\(Wismar\) "de:Heiligen-Geist-Kirche (Wismar)")\] in [Wismar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wismar "Wismar"). (1970 photograph)

Diekmann and Grau gave [Henrik Galeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Galeen "Henrik Galeen"), a disciple of [Hanns Heinz Ewers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanns_Heinz_Ewers "Hanns Heinz Ewers"), the task to write a screenplay inspired by the *Dracula* novel, although Prana Film had not obtained the [film rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_rights "Film rights"). Galeen was an experienced specialist in [dark romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_romanticism "Dark romanticism"); he had already worked on *[The Student of Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Student_of_Prague_\(1913_film\) "The Student of Prague (1913 film)")* (1913), and the screenplay for *[The Golem: How He Came into the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golem:_How_He_Came_into_the_World "The Golem: How He Came into the World")* (1920). Galeen set the story in the fictional north German harbour town of Wisborg. He changed the characters' names and added the idea of the vampire bringing the plague to Wisborg via rats on the ship. Galeen's [Expressionist style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Expressionism_\(cinema\) "German Expressionism (cinema)") screenplay was poetically rhythmic, without being so dismembered as other books influenced by [literary Expressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expressionism_in_literature "Expressionism in literature"), such as those by [Carl Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Mayer "Carl Mayer").
